item.text: {"stage":"answer","question_id":"1B.9","answer":{"question_id":"1B.9","answer":"Target-year evidence is mixed and does not establish a comprehensive, transparently reviewed catastrophic-dual-use safeguards regime personally established by López Obrador. Favorable institutional conduct includes a June 2023 federal agreement creating a Scientific Technical Committee on biosafety of genetically modified organisms, and Mexico’s 2023 participation in regional biological-weapons non-proliferation and biosafety/biosecurity mechanisms, including a 1540 peer review and assistance work. Mexico also issued a 2023 UN statement supporting stronger biological verification, biological-material controls, and scrutiny of emerging technologies, including synthetic biology, biotechnology, and biogenetics. These demonstrate formal engagement and precautionary intent, but the packet does not show the committee’s staffing, budget, enforcement powers, review results, or measurable implementation. Evidence also records international nuclear/radiological safety institutions and regulatory mechanisms operating during or into 2023, including CNSNS oversight, corrective-action systems, emergency exercises, and regulatory responses to two 2023 radioactive-source thefts; these concern nuclear/radiological safety rather than AI or broader dual-use governance, and neither personal presidential direction nor system-wide effectiveness is established. Adverse target-year or directly relevant evidence concerns cyber safeguards. A 2022 Sedena breach exposed more than four million emails; experts linked it to canceled cybersecurity equipment, insufficient personnel, and weak institutional capacity, while López Obrador acknowledged the breach without, in the cited account, addressing the weakness or announcing a remedy. Related reporting described thousands of cyberattack attempts, unpatched and obsolete systems, inadequate monitoring and risk assessment, major military-data exposure, and disruptions affecting public and energy infrastructure. Sedena reportedly implemented updates, strengthened protections, and trained personnel after the breach, but classified its internal investigation and filed no federal criminal complaint; the adequacy and transparency of remediation remain unknown. Further reporting described probable or alleged military-linked Pegasus surveillance of journalists, defenders, and investigators, official denial or minimization, delayed investigation, noncompliance with an INAI disclosure order, and lack of accountability. These are not necessarily catastrophic-dual-use risks in themselves, but they are material evidence of weak cyber-governance transparency, oversight, and accountability under the administration. The 2023 Freedom House evidence likewise reports weakened data-protection and telecommunications regulators, a pending cybersecurity bill with broad takedown and criminal-penalty provisions, risks of militarized cybersecurity, and an INAI quorum crisis after appointments were not made; some judicial decisions preserved safeguards, but those were attributable to courts rather than the ruler. The IMF found progress in financial-sector cybersecurity supervision but continuing resource, autonomy, information-sharing, and consolidated-supervision gaps; this is institutional context rather than direct presidential conduct. Older or later context qualifies the assessment: Mexico had inherited nuclear-safety and biosecurity frameworks, treaty commitments, and formal international positions supporting nonproliferation and safety, but several sources describe unresolved regulatory independence, staffing, knowledge-management, waste-storage, preparedness, and inspection gaps. Later 2024–2025 biosecurity indicators show incomplete expert-review, monitoring, traceability, and information-system coverage, but they cannot prove the 2023 position or be treated as López Obrador-period outcomes. Overall, the record supports formal precautionary commitments and some institutional activity, alongside significant cyber-capacity, transparency, and accountability failures. It does not demonstrate that López Obrador personally established, adequately funded, enforced, and transparently reviewed safeguards across AI, cyber, biological, and other catastrophic dual-use risks;
